The Multitude described there are said to have come from <ns0:hi>Gali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lee, Decapolis, Ierusalem, Iudea,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>beyond Iordan.</ns0:hi> These are said to have come from <ns0:hi>Iudea, Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Sea-coasts of</ns0:hi> Tyre <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Sidon. But thirdly principally from the great difference in the Relations of <ns0:hi>Matthow</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> 1. Many <ns0:hi>large Discour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses</ns0:hi> are not touched by <ns0:hi>Luke, viz.</ns0:hi> Christs whole Discourse in giving a true Interpretation of the Law, his Discourses, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6. about <ns0:hi>Alms, Prayer, Fasting.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> here putteth in three Verses together, wherein there are Woes denounced, of which <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith nothing. Now tho it be usual with the <ns0:hi>Evange<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lists</ns0:hi> to relate the same Discourses, and <ns0:hi>Miracles</ns0:hi> with some di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fferent Circumstances, yet not with such considerable differences, and Variations. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> records nine <ns0:hi>Blessednesses</ns0:hi> pronounced by Christ. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> but four, and those with considerable Varia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion from <ns0:hi>Matthew.</ns0:hi> As for those things which incline some to think it the same Sermon, they do not seem to me Concludent. For what they say as to the Place, it rather proves the contrary. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, it was when he had <ns0:hi>gone up into a Mountain, and sate down. Luke</ns0:hi> saith, he <ns0:hi>was come down,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>stood in the Plain.</ns0:hi> Nor is it more considerable, that most of the passages in this <ns0:hi>Chapter,</ns0:hi> are to be found in the fifth, sixth, or seventh Chapter of <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> for as they are not here exactly repeated according as <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> Recites them. So what should hinder but that our Saviour at another time, and to another Auditory, might Preach the same things which concern all Men. Leaving therefore all to their own Judgments. I see no reason to think that this Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course was but a shorter Copy of the same Discourse, referring to the same time and Company. This being premised, let us now come to consider the Words themselves, comparing them with the Words recited by <ns0:hi>Matthew. Blessed be ye Poor, for yours is the Kindom of God. Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Blessed are the poor in Spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.</ns0:hi> It is true, neither Riches, nor Poverty Bless, or Curse and Man, and none that are Poor are Blessed, if they be <ns0:hi>Proud</ns0:hi> and High-min<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded, nor any Rich Man Cursed, but he that placeth his Portion, or Consolation in Riches, yet Christ here by the <ns0:hi>Antithesis,</ns0:hi> seems more particularly to direct his Discourse, to relieve his Disciples discouraged by their <ns0:hi>Poor,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>low Estate in the World</ns0:hi>; by telling them, that whatever the World thought, they be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his Disciples, believing in him, and following him, were in a better condition than those that were Rich, and had their Conso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation in this Life. <ns0:hi>Blessed are ye that Weep now, for you shall Laugh. Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Blessed are they that Mourn, for they shall be Comforted.</ns0:hi> The Sense is much the same, you that are in a sad afflicted State (being my Disciples) are blessed, for there will come a time when <ns0:hi>God shall wipe Tears from your Eyes. Blessed are you that Hunger, and Thirst, for you shall be filled. Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Blessed are they that Hunger and Thirst after Righteousness.</ns0:hi> It is true, Hungring and Thirsting are no Blessings, but neither are they Curses to a truly Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous Soul, or a Soul that truly seeketh after, and Studyeth Righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness. <ns0:hi>Blessed are ye when Men shall hate you, and when they shall seperate you,</ns0:hi> from their Company, <ns0:hi>and shall Reproach you, and cast out your Name, as Evil, for the Son of Mans sake. Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Blessed are they, which are Persecuted for Righteousness sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Blessed are ye when Men Revile you, and Persecute you, and shall say all manner of Evil against you, falsly for my sake.</ns0:hi> It is true, the general Sense is the same Sufferers, for the Name of Christ are pronounced Blessed, but the Words are very diffe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rent, and here are some <ns0:hi>Species</ns0:hi> of Persecution mentioned, that <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> mentioneth not particularly. 1. <ns0:hi>Separating the Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>Casting out their Names as Evil.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Separating</ns0:hi> here mentioned, may indeed be understood of <ns0:hi>Inprisonment,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Banishment,</ns0:hi> for Persons under those Circumstances are separated from the Company of their relations and Country-men, but it may also be understood of <ns0:hi>Ecclesiastical Censures,</ns0:hi> and thus it agreeth both with our Saviours Prophecy, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 16.2. <ns0:hi>They shall put you out of the Synagogues,</ns0:hi> and with <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 9.22. where we read of a Decree they made, <ns0:hi>that if any did confess that Iesus was the Christ, he should be put out of the Synagogues.</ns0:hi> There are some that think that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> Exercised no such Power till the time of <ns0:hi>Ezra,</ns0:hi> when their Governour was but a Substitute under a <ns0:hi>Pagan Prince,</ns0:hi> who did not give their Conquered Sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects a Power to put any to Death, but left them to Exercise any lighter Punishments. I cannot Subscribe to the Judgment of those Learned Men that think so. For as it is not reasona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able, that God left the Church of the Jews, without that Po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer, that Nature Clotheth every Society with, to purge out of it self such as are not fit Members for it, so it will not enter into my thoughts, that all were to be <ns0:hi>put to Death,</ns0:hi> of whom God said so often, he, or they shall be <ns0:hi>Cut off from his, or their People,</ns0:hi> as in Case of Uncircumcision, not receiving the Passover in its time. So as I do not think that the latter Jews derived this Practice from an humane Constitution, but from a Divine Law. Now we are told that the Jews had three De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees of this <ns0:hi>Separation.</ns0:hi> Some they meerly separated from their Communion, others they <ns0:hi>Anathematized,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>Cursed.</ns0:hi> O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers they so separated, that <ns0:hi>they prayed against them, that God would make them Examples of his Vengeance,</ns0:hi> and some think (but I Judge it but a Guess) that these were those Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners unto Death, for whom <ns0:hi>Iohn would not have Christians Pray.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.16. Now it is certain that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> Exerci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed not the lowest degree only, but the highest against Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians, and also made it their business by Letters, and Word of Mouth to Reproach them all over the World, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 28.22. Now Christ pronounceth them under these Circumstances, <ns0:hi>Blessed, if they suffered these things for his Name sake.</ns0:hi> This casting <ns0:hi>out of their Names as Evil,</ns0:hi> doth not only signify, their blotting out their Names out of the <ns0:hi>Rolls</ns0:hi> of the Church, but the <ns0:hi>defaming of them</ns0:hi> in the manner before mentioned, which was like to be a sore Temptation to the Disciples, against which he further Armeth them, saying, <ns0:hi>Rejoyce ye in that Day, and leap for Ioy, for great is your reward in Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, for in the like manner did their Fathers unto the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets,</ns0:hi> see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.12.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Amos 6.1. James 5.1.</ns0:note> wo unto you that are rich, for ye have received your consolation.<ns0:note place="bottom">Not because you are <ns0:hi>Rich,</ns0:hi> but because you are not Rich to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards God, because you look upon your Riches as your Portion, as your Consolation, or, you that are Rich in the opinion of your own Righteousness.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 65.13.</ns0:note> Wo unto you that are full, for ye shall hun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger.
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:302" />
Wo unto you that laugh now, for ye shall mourn and weep.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour must be understood, either of those who are <ns0:hi>Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully full,</ns0:hi> or at least such as be <ns0:hi>Spiritually empty</ns0:hi>; those that are full, are opposed to those that hunger, if we take <ns0:hi>hunger</ns0:hi> for <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n Hungring and Thirsting after Righteousness, as <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> speaks, those that are full, are such as are filled with Wind, an high opinion of their own Righteousness. If we take <ns0:hi>Hunger</ns0:hi> for a want of the necessaries of this Life, then <ns0:hi>fullness</ns0:hi> signifyeth ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther a <ns0:hi>Sinfulness,</ns0:hi> with Drink, or Meat, or ill gotten Goods, or at least for such as are <ns0:hi>Spiritually</ns0:hi> empty of the Knowledge, or Grace of God; there will come a time when they shall want, as Rich <ns0:hi>Dives</ns0:hi> wanted a little Water to Cool his Tongue. So by those that laugh must be understood, either those that are <ns0:hi>Sinfully</ns0:hi> Merry, or at least those that have no true cause of Spiritual Joy. By <ns0:hi>Mourning</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Weeping</ns0:hi> threatned to such, is either meant the Vengeance of God upon them in this Life, or in the World to come, where there shall be Weeping, and Wailing, and Gnashing of Teeth.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Wo unto you when all men shall speak well of you, for so did their fathers to the false prophets.<ns0:note place="bottom">A good Report of all, even those that are without is a desira<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble thing, and what all good Men ought to Labour for, both by avoiding any just occasion of their speaking ill of them, and by doing all the Acts of Kindness and Charity, that may commend Religion to them. But the World is so Corrupt, that usually none are worse spoken of, then the best Men. And this is true of no sort of Men, more then of the Ministers of the Gospel; neither the <ns0:hi>Prophets of Old,</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> nor Christ, nor the <ns0:hi>Apostles</ns0:hi> could have good Words from the wicked party of their several Ages. The false <ns0:hi>Prophets</ns0:hi> of old, were in much greater Credit with the Generality of the Jews, then the Prophets of the Lord. The Doctrines of the Law, and the Gospel are so contra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry to the most of Mens Lusts, as it is impossible that the most of the World should be Reconciled to it, or to those who faithfully declare it; this the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> in their Age, and the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> and their Friends in our age, have for some time so well understood, that as it was the business of the <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />risees</ns0:hi> in their time, so it hath been the business of the <ns0:hi>Popish Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suists,</ns0:hi> so to Expound the Law of God, as Men may flatter them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, that they are no Debters to it, tho they keep their several Lusts, and so to Interpret the Gospel, that the way to Heaven is made so broad, that it is not easie for any to miss it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.44. Rom. 12.20.</ns0:note> But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Bless them that curse you, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 23.34. Acts 7.60.</ns0:note> pray for them which despitefully use you.<ns0:note place="bottom">We met with these Precepts, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.44. and there Discour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed the Sense of them. See the Notes there.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.39, 40.</ns0:note> And unto him that smiteth thee on the <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> cheek, offer also the other, and him that taketh a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 6.7.</ns0:note> thy cloak, forbid not <ns0:hi>to take thy</ns0:hi> coat also.<ns0:note place="bottom">We met also with a passage much like this, in this Verse, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.39. the General Sense of which was, as I then said, A <ns0:hi>Prohibition of private Revenge.</ns0:hi> It is therefore there pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faced in with a more general Precept, <ns0:hi>Resist not Evil.</ns0:hi> But be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sides this there seems to be in it also a Prohibition of vexatious Suits and Molestations of others, tho under a Colour of Law, therefore <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>If any Man will sue thee at Law, and take away thy Cloak</ns0:hi>; and it may be thought a more special Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept relating to those times, when they had none but <ns0:hi>Heathen Magistrates,</ns0:hi> and in some Measure to be expounded by, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.7. and to be a Precept given with respect to the <ns0:hi>Reputation of the Gospel,</ns0:hi> that it might not be Scandalized by Christians, <ns0:hi>going to Law before Infidels.</ns0:hi> It is most certain it doth not for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bid the use of the Law, whether for the defending, or recovering our just Rights, only the <ns0:hi>Irregular, or Scandalous use of it</ns0:hi>; see further the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.39.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Give to every man that asketh of thee, and of him that taketh away thy goods, ask <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> not again.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> hath much the same passage, only he saith <ns0:hi>Give to him that,</ns0:hi> &c. not to <ns0:hi>every one that asketh of thee,</ns0:hi> and for the latter Clause, he hath <ns0:hi>from him that would borrow of thee, turn not away thine Hand,</ns0:hi> which seems more agreeing to the Precept, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 15.8. These Precepts of our Saviour must be interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, not according to the strict Sense of the Words, as if every Man were by them obliged, without regard to his own Abilities, or Circumstances of Persons begging, or asking of him, to give to every one that hath the Confidence to ask of him, but as obliging us to Liberality, and Charity, according to our Abilities, and the true Needs, and Circumstances of our poor Brethren, and in that order which Gods Word hath directed us; first, providing for our own Families, then doing good to the Houshold of Faith, then also to others, as we are able, and see any of them true Ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects of our Charity. Nor must the second part of the Verse be interpreted; as if it were a restraint of Christians, from pursuing of Thieves, or Oppressors, but as a Precept, prohibiting us pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate Revenge, or too great contending for little things, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.42.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.12. This is the Law of Nature, the Golden Rule of all Justice, and may also serve for a Guide to us to expound the former Verses, and some other Precepts of Charity in this Chapter. Men in all these Cases should consider what they would be glad, and think reasonable that others should do to them, were they in their Circumstances, and the others had the same Ability, or advantage to do good to them, and by this they should measure their Acts both of Justice, and Charity.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.42.</ns0:note> And if ye lend to them of whom ye hope to receive, what thank have ye? for sinners also lend to sinners, to receive as much again.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.46, 47. The Strength of our Saviours Argument lyeth in this, That God expecteth, that those who have received more Grace, and favour from God then others, and who make an higher profession than others, should do more in obedience to the Positive Commands of God, and the Revelations of his Will in his Word, then they who Live meer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly by the light of nature, and live up meerly to the Law of Nature.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again, and your reward shall be great, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.44, 45.48.</ns0:note> ye shall be the children of the highest, for he is kind unto the unthankful, and <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> the evil.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 Be ye therefore merciful, as your father also is merciful.<ns0:note place="bottom">I know not how to agree what I find many Interpreters judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, that this Text is a <ns0:hi>Prohibition</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Vsury.</ns0:hi> I should ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther interpret it more largely, as a <ns0:hi>Command</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Acts of Mercy,</ns0:hi> with respect to the Circumstances of Persons, obliging us not to with-hold a Charitable Hand, from our fear, that if we lend we shall lose what we lend, and obliging us, that if we find the Circumstances of any, that desireth us to lend him for his neces<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sity, such a quantity of Money or Goods as we can spare, and we can well enough bear the loss of, if the Providence of God should render the Person unable to repay us, we should not be awed by such a fear from Acts of Charity, but give with a Resolu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to lose it, if God please to disable the Person to whom we lend, so as he cannot repay us. For the question about <ns0:hi>Vsury,</ns0:hi> as to which some conceive this Text a <ns0:hi>Prohibition,</ns0:hi> this is not a place to handle it in the Latitude. I do not think it was ever absolutely forbidden to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> they might take it of <ns0:hi>Stran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers,</ns0:hi> and that not only of the <ns0:hi>Canaanites,</ns0:hi> whom some say they might kill (which I doubt after their agreement to a quiet Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />habitation) but of other Strangers also who came not under the Denomination of <ns0:hi>Canaanites.</ns0:hi> That argued the taking of Usury to be not <ns0:hi>malum per se,</ns0:hi> in its self evil, but only <ns0:hi>malum prohibitum,</ns0:hi> an Evil as forbidden, and not absolutely, <ns0:hi>and universally for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bidden,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>respectively,</ns0:hi> only with reference to their Brethren of the same Church, and Nation, so rather to be reckoned amongst the <ns0:hi>Municipal Laws</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> than the Commons Laws of God for all Mankind. Besides that amongst the Jews there was less need of it, partly in respect of their Years of <ns0:hi>Iubilee,</ns0:hi> and partly in regard their imployments were chiefly in Husbandry, and about Cattle, which called not for such Sums of Money, as Merchandizing doth. Nor is it to be referred to any of the <ns0:hi>Ten Commandements, unless the Seventh, Thou shalt not Steal,</ns0:hi> which forbidding Sins against <ns0:hi>Charity,</ns0:hi> and such Sins against Charity being there forbidden, as are <ns0:hi>The taking away the Goods of another against their Will, and without a just cause,</ns0:hi> I cannot see, How the lending of Money for a moderate use, when it is helpful, and relieving to our Neighbour, should be any <ns0:hi>kind of Stealing,</ns0:hi> when his good Will appeareth in the Contract; nor can there be any injustice in it, where there is a <ns0:hi>Quid pro quo,</ns0:hi> but a Proportion for what I am indammaged by the loan; un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less any will say it is <ns0:hi>unjustly,</ns0:hi> because <ns0:hi>against the Law of God,</ns0:hi> which is to beg the Question, this Argument being brought to prove it is not contrary to the Law of God. The Exacting of an un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />due Proportion for <ns0:hi>Vsury,</ns0:hi> or a moderate Proportion, when we plainly see, our Brother is fallen into Poverty, and cannot pay it, may be forbidden, as a Sin against Charity, and that love that we ought to shew to our Neighbours, and the <ns0:hi>Mercifulness</ns0:hi> here re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 36. yet, admitting the Law of God, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23.19, 20. to be interpreted of all <ns0:hi>Vsury,</ns0:hi> (which yet seemeth hard,) for then the Jews might not sell for any thing more at twelve Months time, then if they were paid presently, for the Words are <ns0:hi>Vsury of Money, Vsury of Victuals, Vsury of any thing lent upon Vsury</ns0:hi>) it concerned the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> only, betwixt themselves, not in their dealings with any Strangers, which is plain, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. so also. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22.25. where the Term <ns0:hi>Poor</ns0:hi> is also put in as it is, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 25.35, 36, 37. By which Texts the <ns0:hi>Psalmist</ns0:hi> must be expounded, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 15.5. It may possibly from the Equity of that Law oblige us, to be more kind to those that are of the same Nation and Church with us, then unto others, especially such as are no Christians; and amongst those that are Christians, to those that are Poor, then to those who have better Estates. But as I said in the beginning, I had rather interpret the Precept of the Text more largely, as a general precept of Mercy, from the <ns0:hi>Example</ns0:hi> of our Heavenly Father.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:303" />37 Judge not, and ye shall not be judged, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demn not, and ye shall not be condemned, forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.1. and on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.14. where we have discoursed, what private <ns0:hi>Iudgings</ns0:hi> are here <ns0:hi>forbidden,</ns0:hi> and what <ns0:hi>forgiving</ns0:hi> is here required.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 19.17.</ns0:note> Give, and it shall be given unto you, good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosome. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 7.2.</ns0:note> For with the same measure that ye mete withal, it shall be measured to you again.<ns0:note place="bottom">To let us know how God favoureth Acts of Charity and Justice we shall observe, that there are no good Deeds, that God so rewardeth by <ns0:hi>Retaliation,</ns0:hi> as such which are the Products of these Habits, nor <ns0:hi>any Sins,</ns0:hi> which God so punisheth by way of <ns0:hi>Retaliations,</ns0:hi> as Sins contrary to these, especially such as are more eminently contrary. This Verse speaks of <ns0:hi>Acts of Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity. Give, and it shall be given to you,</ns0:hi> and that not bare mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure, but good Measure, Pressed down, and shaken together, and running over; nothing can more Concur to make good Mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure, than the shaking of the Bushel, the Crouding and Pressing down of the Corn, or Meal with the Hand, and the Pouring in till the Measure runneth over. So as that which is here promi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed, is a plentiful reward to Charitable and Merciful Actions, either from the Hand of God more <ns0:hi>Mediately,</ns0:hi> God stirring up others to be as kind to us as we are to others, or more <ns0:hi>immediately</ns0:hi> him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self Blessing us by his inexpected Providential Dispensations; to this purpose are abundance of Scriptures, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24.19. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 41.1, 2, 3. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 11.25. and 28.27. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9.6. If Men will not be so just, as to requite the good which their Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren have done them, having it in their Power, yet God will be faithful to his Promises, and by his Providence take care, that those who have done Acts of Mercy, not in a meer Commise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration to Humane Condition, but in a just obedience to his Will, shall not lose by what they have done, they shall be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />warded fully and plentifully, finding again (tho it may be af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter many days) the Bread which they have cast upon the Waters, according to his command.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 And he spake a parable unto them, Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?<ns0:note place="bottom">By a <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> here is to be understood a Proverbial saying, which hath some darkness in it, as being brought to express, or signify more than the Words naturally do express. Proverbial Speeches, are applicable to more things, and in more Cases than one. Nor is it to be expected, that in all that the Evangelists give us an account of, as to the sayings of Christ, we should be able to find out an evident Connexion. They (questionless) Wrote much at least from their Memories, and set down many sayings, without respect to the time when our Saviour spake them, or the matter of his Discourse, immediately preceding them; we need not therefore be careful to make out the Connexion of these Words of his, with what was before set down, in the <ns0:hi>Paralel</ns0:hi> Text, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.14. Our Saviour plainly applyeth these Words with reference to the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> the Jewish Leaders, their <ns0:hi>Doctors,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi> at that time, who themselves being ignorant of the true Sense of the Divine Law, were not like very well to Guide others, but with them <ns0:hi>to fall into the Ditch</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that is, into Ruin and Destruction, from whence a very probable <ns0:hi>Connexion</ns0:hi> of them here, with what went before may be observed; for as appears from <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5. he had in the preceding Verses, given an interpretation of that Law of God. <ns0:hi>Thou shalt love thy Neighbour as thy self,</ns0:hi> much different form what the Pharisees had given of it, who had expounded it, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.43. <ns0:hi>Thou shalt love thy Neighbour, and hate thy Enemy.</ns0:hi> Making a great many Branches of Love to Men, more than they made Now (saith he) This is the Will, this is the Law of my Heavenly Father. The <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> your present <ns0:hi>Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctors</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi> go much below this, but listen not to them, if you mind to please God; themselves are Blind, and know not the Will of God, and if you follow them, what can you ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pect more than such an event, as where one Blind Man leads a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nother.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 The disciple is not above his master, but every <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 5.48.</ns0:note> one that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>shall be perfected as his master.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> is perfect shall be as his master.<ns0:note place="bottom">This was another common saying, which our Saviour apply<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.24. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 15.20. to comfort his Disciples con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning their Sufferings, because he was first in Suffering: here he applyeth it to signify their Duty <ns0:hi>in doing.</ns0:hi> Some apply this with reference to the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> and so make a Connexion betwixt this and the former Verse, where he had said, <ns0:hi>If the Blind lead the Blind, they shall both fall into the Ditch.</ns0:hi> For, <ns0:hi>The Disciple is not above his Master,</ns0:hi> none must look to learn of another, more than the Teacher knoweth himself. But it is better ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plyed to Christ, and is as much as if our Lord had said, I am your Master, you are my Disciples, and by that Relation<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> inga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged to learn of me, and to follow me. I have taught you no more than I am ready to practise, I am <ns0:hi>Merciful,</ns0:hi> I forgive, I give, looking for nothing again. I do not look that you should do any thing above me: any thing as to which I have not set you, or shall not set you an Example, but your perfection lyeth in coming as near to me as you can, in being as your Master.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brothers eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 Either how canst thou say to thy brother, Brother, let me pull out the mote that is in thine eye, when thou thy self beholdest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>See</ns0:hi> Prov. 18.17.</ns0:note> cast out first the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to pull out the mote that is in thy bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers eye.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.3, 4, 5.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit, neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 12.33.</ns0:note> every tree is known by his own fruit, for of thorns men do not gather figs, not of a bramble<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bush gather <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. a <ns0:hi>grape.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> they grapes.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 12.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> A good man out of the good treasure of his heart, bringeth forth that which is good, and an e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vil man out of the evil treasure of his heart, bringeth forth that which is evil, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 12.34.</ns0:note> of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.16, 17, 18.20. The 43. and 44. are expounded in the 45. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> Men and Women here, (as in o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Texts of Scripture) are compared to <ns0:hi>Trees</ns0:hi> with respect to their <ns0:hi>Root</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Fruit,</ns0:hi> and the dependance the <ns0:hi>Fruit</ns0:hi> hath upon the Root, and the Nature of the Tree. The <ns0:hi>Heart</ns0:hi> of Man is made the Root, that being the Principle of humane Actions, as the Root is the Principle to the Fruit; for all the overt Actions of a Mans Life, are but the imperate Acts of the Heart and of the Will. Hence it is that a Will renewed and Sanctifyed in a Man and made Conformable to the Will of God, doth not only will, and chuse the Will of God, love it, desire it, and delight in it, but commandeth the Tongue to direct its Discourses conformable to it, and also commandeth all the Members of their Body, in their Motions, and Order, to Act conformably; and on the contrary the unrenewed, and sanctifyed Will of Man, doth not only reject, and refuse the Will of God, but directeth the Tongue to Words contrary to the Divine Will, and all the Members of the Body in their Motions and Order, to act without any respect to, or aw of the Will of God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 1.6. Mat. 7.21. Chap. 13.25.</ns0:note> And why call ye me Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings, and doth them, I will shew you to whom he is like.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 He is like a man which built an house, and dig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock, and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it, for it was founded upon a rock.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 But he that heareth and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth, against which the stream did beat vehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mently, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.24, 25, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> where we before met with the same thing. The Sum is, Mens Hopes of Salvation builded upon any other but Christ alone, or Builded upon Christ, without a Sincere Study, and Indeavour to keep the Command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of Christ, are Vain Hopes, and tho till a Storm of <ns0:hi>Afflicti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Temptation</ns0:hi> comes, they may please themselves a little with them, yet when they come to dy, or when any notable Tempta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion assaults them, or any great Affliction cometh upon them, then they will fail them, and they will see the folly, and Vanity of them, <ns0:hi>what is the Hope of the Hypocrite, when God takes away his Soul?</ns0:hi> Job 27.8.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
